Article Title: 31 years ago, Ganesha ‘drank’ milk and India went viral: How a September 21, 1995 claim spread from temple to temple, crossed borders within hours and became a global story without social media

And somehow, by the end of that extraordinary day, a spoonful of milk had become a global story.

Thirty-one years ago, on September 21, 1995, I came home from school to find that something was strangely different. My aunt, who would diligently wait for me every day and was always the one to serve me lunch, was missing. She was more than just the person who fed me; she would sit with me, tell me interesting stories and make the afternoon feel special.I looked for her everywhere. Finally, the housemaid arrived with my plate of dal and rice and casually told me, “Didi has gone to feed milk to Lord Ganesha.”I was puzzled. What did she mean? After lunch, I called a friend from the landline. She had the same story. Her mother, too, was not at home. By evening, my aunt returned, visibly excited, and told my mother, who had just come back from work, what she had seen.“I took a spoon of milk to feed Ganesha, and the milk disappeared,” she said. My mother looked at her in disbelief. “Really?” she asked. “Really. I saw it with my own eyes,” she insisted, quite overwhelmed with emotions.The news spread fast, Ganesha idols were apparently drinking milk. There were no smartphones, social media platforms, WhatsApp groups or instant notifications to amplify the news.India’s internet had only just arrived, television was still dominated by Doordarshan, and newspapers remained the primary source of next-day news. Yet, within hours, temples were overflowing, milk was disappearing from shops and the story had travelled beyond India.It was not the age of viral news. In fact viral was the world synonymous with just one thing-the infectious disease of influenza. There was no way to immediately search the internet, watch a viral video or check social media posts from another city. Then what caused the spread of this frenzy? According to a contemporary Times of India report Mumbai and several other parts of India were swept by reports that Ganesha idols were accepting milk offerings. The report described the news as spreading “like wildfire” as thousands of devotees rushed to temples.The crucial point was that people did not merely hear the claim. They went to temples and tried it for themselves. Devotees carried spoons filled with milk towards the trunks or mouths of Ganesha idols, and many reported seeing the milk disappear.The episode becomes even more extraordinary when viewed against India's technological landscape in 1995. Public internet access had only just been launched by VSNL in August that year. According to historicalinternet use in India in 1995 stood at just 0.026% of the population.Telephones were also far from universal. India had approximately 11.98 million fixed telephone connections in 1995, equivalent to around 1.24 fixed lines per 100 people.This meant that the mechanisms of mass communication were fundamentally different from those available today. A person could call a relative, but there was no instant group messaging system through which hundreds of people could receive the same information simultaneously. News moved through conversations, local networks, religious communities, radio, television and newspapers. And yet the Ganesha story moved extraordinarily quickly.It would be inaccurate to suggest that India had only Doordarshan in 1995. The country's television landscape had already begun changing. Zee TV had launched in 1992, Star TV had entered the Indian market in 1991 and Sony Entertainment Television launched in 1995. But the explosion of private, round-the-clock news channels that would later transform India's news culture was still years away.Doordarshan nevertheless remained hugely influential . An academic study citing Ministry of Information & Broadcasting figures puts India's television universe in 1995 at approximately 40 million television households and 250 million viewers.There was therefore a very different relationship between an event and the news cycle. Newspapers generally reported what had happened the previous day, television had scheduled programming rather than today's constant breaking-news stream, and there was no digital ecosystem continuously refreshing itself. The Ganesha phenomenon had to travel through people before it could become a mass media story.The reports quickly produced visible consequences. A contemporary Los Angeles Times repor published on September 23, 1995, said millions of Indians had rushed to test the phenomenon and reported that milk had “virtually disappeared” from shops in New Delhi by noon.That detail captures the extraordinary feedback loop created by the phenomenon. People heard that Ganesha was drinking milk, went out to buy milk, took it to temples and offered it to idols. The resulting rush itself became evidence of how seriously the story was being taken.Contemporary reports described crowds gathering at temples, with devotees carrying spoons, bowls and containers of milk.The most remarkable part of the episode was perhaps how quickly it crossed India's borders. Reports soon emerged from Hindu communities in Britain, the United States, Canada, Nepal and elsewhere. A contemporary os Angeles Times report noted that the reports had spread beyond India to Hindu communities in other countries, including Britain and Los Angeles. Hinduism Today later recalled receiving telephone calls and fax messages from different parts of the world reporting similar experiences. Its contemporary account provides a fascinating glimpse into how an international religious community communicated before email, social media and messaging apps became commonplace.The technology may appear primitive by today's standards, but the human network was remarkably effective. Someone in India could telephone a relative abroad, that person could contact a local temple, and within hours another community could be trying the same experiment.The story did not need an algorithm to travel. It travelled through relationships.As the reports spread, scientists and sceptics began examining what devotees were observing. One of the principal scientific explanations involved capillary action and surface tension. Rather than the idol literally consuming the milk, the liquid could move along the surface of the material, creating the appearance that it was being absorbed by the idol.For devotees, however, the scientific explanation did not necessarily invalidate what they had experienced. The same physical observation could be interpreted through very different frameworks: as a religious sign by believers, as a scientific phenomenon by researchers, and as an extraordinary mass social event by journalists.Looking back from the age of smartphones, the 1995 episode is remarkable not simply because of what people believed they were seeing, but because of how quickly the information travelled.India's public internet had only just begun. Fixed telephone connections were limited, television was expanding but had not yet become the 24-hour news environment of today, and newspapers operated on a fundamentally different news cycle. Yet within hours, a local report had become a national phenomenon and then an international story.A telephone call led to another telephone call. A conversation at one temple led to another. Newspapers carried the story forward, television added another layer of coverage and international media transformed what had begun as a local religious phenomenon into a global news story.Calling the Ganesha milk episode the world's first viral phenomenon would be too absolute. Stories travelled internationally long before 1995, through newspapers, radio, television and word of mouth.But the episode offers a remarkable case study of mass communication before the social-media era. Millions of people participated in the same rapidly spreading story without having access to the tools that today make such mass participation almost instantaneous.That is what makes September 21, 1995, worth remembering 31 years later. The question is no longer simply whether Ganesha idols were actually drinking milk. The episode has another story to tell, about technology, faith, communication and human networks.In 2026, information can travel around the world in seconds. In 1995, it travelled from person to person, from telephone to telephone, from temple to temple and eventually from newspaper to newspaper.(All images are AI Generated)
Article Summary: In 1995, india was still largely offline. There were no smartphones, social media platforms, whatsapp groups or instant notifications to amplify the news. Within hours, temples were overflowing, milk was disappearing from shops and the story had travelled beyond india.

Article Title: Govt asks people to use Sanchar Saathi to verify mobile connections, handsets
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Govt Monday asked people to verify their mobile connections through the Sanchar Saathi Portal (http://www.sancharsaathi.gov.in), which allows them to check all numbers issued in their name and block those that are unnecessary or not genuinely theirs. The advice from the dept of telecom (DoT) came after a cybercrime probe led to a point of sale for SIM cards in Chhattisgarh where the agent was found to have illegally activated 25 mobile connections (SIMs) using citizens’ identification documents without their knowledge or consent.“Following this, the DoT and telecom service providers immediately blacklisted the concerned (agent), preventing it from issuing mobile connections (SIMs) in the future. These 25 mobile connections were examined.. Numbers failing re-verification were deactivated,” DoT said in a statement.It reiterated that “fraudulent issuance of SIM cards, misuse of telecom identifiers, or tampering with IMEI numbers is a punishable offence under the Telecommunications Act, 2023. Such violations may attract imprisonment of up to three years and fines up to Rs 50 lakh.”“Citizens are cautioned not to share or transfer SIM cards issued in their name, as legal liability may extend to the original subscriber if the SIM is found to be misused. To safeguard themselves, citizens are advised to regularly verify their mobile connections through the Sanchar Saathi Portal ( http://www.sancharsaathi.gov.in) and Mobile App. The platform enables users to check all mobile numbers issued in their name and block those that are unnecessary or not genuinely theirs.These measures are significant to prevent misuse of telecom resources in cyber frauds and to ensure a safe and secure communication environment,” it added.Misuse of SIMs, telecommunication identifiers, including International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) number of mobile devices “has emerged as a matter of serious concern” with the rapid expansion of mobile connectivity and digital services across India.“Citizens can access various services available under Sanchar Saathi to verify and protect their mobile connections and devices. Citizens are urged to remain vigilant and make use of the digital tools available through the Sanchar Saathi initiative to verify and secure their mobile handsets. The IMEI details of a mobile handset can be verified through the Sanchar Saathi platform by using Check Genuineness of Your Mobile handset facility. The service enables citizens to check details such as the brand name, model name and manufacturer information associated with the device,” it said.
Article Summary: The advice from the dept of telecom (dot) came after a cybercrime probe led to a point of sale for sim cards in chhattisgarh. The agent was found to have illegally activated 25 mobile connections (sims) using citizens’ identification documents.

Article Title: UPI MDR row: NCP (SP) demands rollback of 0.4% charge, calls it ‘assault’ on small traders
Article Text:
Calls MDR a burden on small traders

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The NCP (SP) on Monday demanded a complete rollback of the 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on specified UPI merchant transactions above Rs 2,000, calling the move a “direct assault” on small traders and shopkeepers.NCP (SP) state spokesperson Mahesh Tapase alleged that the decision reflected “double standards” by the Narendra Modi government, questioning why small merchants were being made to bear additional costs while large industrialists had benefited from loan write-offs, news agency PTI reported.The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has announced that a 0.4% MDR will apply from October 15 to specified person-to-merchant UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, with the charge capped at Rs 300 per transaction. Person-to-person transactions will remain free. Payments to merchants up to Rs 2,000 and transactions covered under the zero-MDR framework for small merchants will also remain free.Tapase said small traders, shopkeepers and street vendors had played a key role in building the country's UPI ecosystem and questioned the rationale for imposing the charge on them.“For years, this government told the nation that Digital India and UPI were gifts to the common man — free, instant and empowering.Now, the moment UPI becomes the backbone of India's retail economy, the Modi government has quietly reached into the pockets of the very small businessmen who made it a success,” he said.He also alleged that the government was following “double standards” in financial matters, claiming that large industrialists had benefited from loan write-offs while small traders were being asked to bear additional costs.“This is not policy... This is betrayal,” Tapase alleged.
Article Summary: The national payments corporation of india has announced that a 0.4% mdr will apply from october 15 to specified person-to-merchant upi transactions above rs 2,000. Ncp (sp) state spokesperson mahesh tapase alleged that the decision reflected “double standards” by the narendra modi government.

Article Title: Govt dissolves digital communications commission with immediate effect
Article Text:
Govt has dissolved its apex decision-making body for telecom and digital communication. (Representative image)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Governmnet has with immediate effect dissolved its apex decision-making body for telecom and digital communication — digital communications commission (DCC), which was originally established as telecom commission in 1989 before being renamed in 2018.The communication ministry’s dept of telecommunications notified this decision through a Sept 19, 2026, resolution that was published in the Gazette of India, Monday “with effect from the date of publication of this resolution, the DCC shall stand dissolved,” says the gazette.Decisions for projects upto Rs 100 crore can be taken by the secretary DoT, upto Rs 500 crore by the telecom minister and those above Rs 500 crore to Rs 1,000 were considered by the DCC. Now the same will be referred to the expenditure finance committee, inter-ministerial body under finmin’s dept of expenditure which will evaluate the same before being submitted to the cabinet for formal approval.“The decision was notified last week. DCCA used to have chairman (secretary DoT) and three members. Now that structure will be replaced by an advisor in the ministry. Those changes are being made,” said people aware of the matter.The gazette dissolving DCC traces its history. It was set up as telecom commission in April 1989 to “deal with various aspects relating to the telecommunications sector.” It was re-designated as DCC in October 2018.
Article Summary: Govt has dissolved its apex decision-making body for telecom and digital communication. Digital communications commission (dcc) was originally established as telecom commission in 1989 before being renamed in 2018. Decisions for projects upto rs 100 crore can be taken by the secretary dot, upto £500 by the telecom minister.

Article Title: In 2013, Canadian teenager Ann Makosinski invented a flashlight powered by body heat; now she is creating colourful toys to teach children about renewable energy
Article Text:
A new kind of light

eDrink : A mug that generates electricity

Toys with renewable energy

They say some children are born prodigies, and when it comes to Ann Makosinski, the statement holds true. As a teenager living in Canada, her friend living in the Philippines told her that she couldn't study at night since her family couldn't afford electricity to turn the lights on. Soon she wondered if there was a way to have light without traditional electricity. This is when she came up with a record-making invention, a flashlight powered by body heat.Like other children her age, Makosinski did not watch television or play video games. She spent her time listening to the opera, watching silent movies and learning to play the piano and violin. Interestingly, her first toy was a box of transistors. “I wasn’t given many toys, so I had to make my own,” she said to CNN back in 2019. “I would take garbage and my hot glue gun from around the house and piece together these so-called inventions, and obviously they never worked, but the idea of taking things from around me and piecing them together to make something better just kind of came really naturally. ”Makosinski was only 15 when she invented a flashlight that was powered by the heat of the user's hands.The Hollow Flashlight uses thermoelectric technology to convert the temperature difference between the user's hand and the surrounding air into electricity. The device uses Peltier tiles, which generate electricity when one side is heated by the palm of the hand and the other is cooled.No batteries are required, with the flashlight running entirely on human body heat that would otherwise go to waste. School students, therefore, could study without worrying about running out of battery power.The Hollow Flashlight earned Makosinski a win in the 15-16 age category at the 2013 Google Science Fair and won at the 2014 Intel International Science and Engineering Fair. Her wins made her an international media sensation. She made appearances on shows such as 'The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon' and was featured in publications such as TIME and Forbes. She even gave a TEDxTeen Talk titled 'Why I don't use a smartphone'. Makosinski only bought her first phone, an old-fashioned flip model, at the age of 18.The intrigued teenager did not stop there. Soon, she launched her next major invention, the eDrink. At 18, while enrolled at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, she designed a coffee mug to capture the excess heat from a hot beverage and convert it into electricity. This excess energy could then be used to provide a small charge to a phone or other device for 30 minutes. It uses Peltier tiles (thermoelectric generators), and by heating one side of the tiles with your drink and cooling the other side with the design of the mug (and a bunch of electronic circuits, of course), electricity is produced."I got the inspiration for my project when I noticed that my high school friends were always complaining about their phones dying too soon and that their coffee was too hot to drink," she told Society for Science.Now 29, Makosinski is looking to inspire other young girls across the world to use their minds and creativity in a similar fashion. Her interest in thermoelectric technology has led her toward a different kind of invention: toys designed to teach children about renewable energy.She has created bright-coloured toys that help kids learn about renewable energy in exciting ways. They can see and play with it as it lights up, spins or makes sound when powered by sunlight, water or a hand-wound mechanism.The goal now, she told CNN, is to have other youngsters, girls in particular, follow her into the world of science.“I just want, especially young kids, to feel like they can invent their own solutions and they don’t have to wait for other people to make them,” said Makosinski, who described herself as “a normal girl who just used her time differently after school.”“I want to inspire people to be more creative with the resources they have around them,” she added.
Article Summary: Ann makosinski was 15 when she invented a flashlight powered by body heat. At 18, she designed a coffee mug to capture the excess heat from a hot beverage and convert it into electricity. Now 29, she is looking to inspire other young girls across the world to use their minds and creativity in a similar fashion.

Article Title: Caitlin Clark’s $20M fortune gets attention, but her $100,000+ cereal campaign reveals a different side of her WNBA success and community work
Article Text:
Caitlin Clark’s $20M fortune gets attention, but her $100,000+ cereal campaign reveals a different side of her WNBA success and community work (Image via Getty: Caitlin Clark)

How did Caitlin Clark’s cereal campaign raise more than $100,000 for youth programmes?

Caitlin Clark’s $20M fortune is only one part of her story away from basketball

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Caitlin Clark’s rise in women’s basketball has brought plenty of attention to her growing profile off the court. One of the more unusual examples came through a box of cereal, as her Caitlin’s Crunch Time partnership with Hy-Vee turned a popular food product into a fundraising effort for young people.The campaign raised more than $100,000 for the Caitlin Clark Foundation, with the money supporting programmes centred on education, nutrition and sports across the Midwest. It offered fans a simple way to connect with Clark’s community work while supporting causes linked closely to her foundation.Per Caitlin Clark foundation website, the idea began as a partnership between Clark, her foundation and Hy-Vee. Caitlin’s Crunch Time cereal returned to Hy-Vee stores across the Midwest in May 2025 after an earlier limited release in Iowa. Hy-Vee pledged a percentage of the proceeds from each box sold to the Caitlin Clark Foundation.The partnership had a personal connection to Clark’s own story. Her foundation focuses on three areas: education, nutrition and sports, which it describes as pillars that played an important role in her development as an athlete. The cereal campaign gave fans a simple way to support that work while buying a product connected to Clark.“Having my own cereal is a fun way to connect with fans,” Clark said when Hy-Vee announced the 2025 release. She also thanked the company for supporting the foundation and its mission to improve the lives of young people.By Jan. 2026, the foundation announced that the campaign had raised more than $100,000. It said the funds would help support local initiatives across the Midwest, giving the campaign a purpose beyond the product itself.The partnership also forms part of a longer relationship between Clark and Hy-Vee. The foundation said the company had raised approximately $500,000 for its work through its partnership with Clark.Clark’s commercial rise has been rapid since she became one of the biggest names in women’s basketball. Celebrity Net Worth currently estimates her net worth at $20 million and lists her 2026 WNBA salary at roughly $530,000. The site also reports that she earned about $16 million from endorsements in 2025 and has an estimated $28 million Nike deal running over eight years.Those figures show the scale of Clark’s success away from the basketball court, but the cereal campaign offers a different look at how that commercial profile can be connected to her foundation’s work.The campaign was not simply a personal $100,000 donation from Clark. The more than $100,000 figure represents money raised through Caitlin's Crunch Time campaign, while Hy-Vee provided the retail platform and pledged proceeds to the foundation.That distinction is important because Clark’s community work often involves partnerships that turn her popularity into support for youth programmes. Her foundation says its goal is to create opportunities for children to learn, grow and thrive through education, nutrition and sports.In Clarks’ case, the cereal became more than a piece of merchandise. It connected her growing commercial profile with a cause that sits at the centre of her foundation’s work, while giving fans another way to participate in that effort.
Article Summary: Caitlin clark’s $20m fortune gets attention, but her $100,000+ cereal campaign reveals a different side of her wnba success and community work. Her crunch time partnership with hy-vee turned a popular food product into a fundraising effort for young people. The money supporting programmes centred on education, nutrition and sports across the midwest.

Article Title: Fake Apple centre in Gurgaon ‘shortlisted’ elderly in US, scared them into paying up to $20k
Article Text:
Elderly US citizens were targeted with fake privacy and virus warnings (Representative image generated using AI)

Fake Apple centre in Gurgaon ‘shortlisted’ elderly in US





GURGAON: The sham Apple service centre busted in Palam Vihar on Sept 1 did not wait for victims to call. Its operator first screened targets in the US, checked whether they were above 60 and had substantial bank balances, and sent warning messages about privacy, virus or technical problems in their iPhones.The elderly victims, with little technical knowhow, were then funnelled into calls where impersonators invoked a bogus Federal Trade Commission (FTC) notice and demanded $10,000 to $20,000 to fix the issues — amounts far exceeding the price of a brand new iPhone.The operation allegedly began with messages routed through a server controlled by Jai Kakkar, a Delhi resident who police have identified as its operator.The messages directed recipients to a toll-free number connected to the Palam Vihar call centre. Police have so far traced transactions worth $200,000 (around Rs 2 crore), which was fleeced from 15 US citizens allegedly targeted over eight to 10 days.The scam then involved two stages. A less experienced caller first posed as an Apple customer care executive, telling the victim that their device had a problem.Once the victim was convinced, the call was transferred to a senior posing as a banker.The second caller allegedly produced a fake FTC notice and used the threat to demand payment.“The first caller, who would often be less experienced, would establish contact by posing as an Apple executive.Once the victim was convinced, the call was transferred to a caller posing as a banker, who would introduce the fake FTC notice and make the payment demand,” an officer said.Police said victims were asked to transfer the money to a foreign bank account. In some cases, they allegedly obtained gift card or voucher numbers. Callers at the centre received commissions of 11% to 16% for each successful scam.The profiling was central to the operation. “The gang checked if potential targets were senior citizens and had substantial bank balances. The elderly usually have less technical knowledge,” a senior officer said. Police are still trying to establish the source of the database and how the accused obtained such information.Police said an examination of laptops seized from the centre showed the initial messages were routed through the operator’s server.One laptop contained data from the previous 10 days, while other details had been erased or shifted elsewhere. “An average of 40 calls were made on a daily basis,” an officer said.The bogus service centre had come up in a house in J block of Palam Vihar. A 14-member team under ACP (cyber) Gaurav Fogat and SHO (Cyber West) Sombir arrested 11 persons and seized nine laptops, 20 mobile phones, two headphone-and-mic sets, two cars, a motorcycle and a scooter.Police said X-Lite Dialler and Apple FaceTime were used to communicate with victims.Kakkar is yet to be traced. Police searched his Model Town house but did not find him. “The source would be unearthed once Kakkar is arrested.Teams are working to trace him and the money trail,” a police source said. Police are also checking his alleged role in an earlier Delhi cheating case and alleged links to other cybercrime operations.
Article Summary: Elderly us citizens were targeted with fake privacy and virus warnings. Police have so far traced transactions worth $200,000 (around rs 2 crore), which was fleeced from 15 us citizens allegedly targeted over eight to 10 days. An average of 40 calls were made on a daily basis, an officer said.

Googlebook features

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu to engineers: Use AI but never ...
Article Text:
Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu to engineers: Use AI but never ...

Engineer says AI is changing software development

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has warned engineers against relying too heavily on artificial intelligence for software development. In an X post, Sridhar Vembu said that engineers should use AI tools without giving up their own understanding of the work. Vembu was responding to a post by a software engineer who described the use of Anthropic's Claude Code at a large company. The engineer claimed that AI was being used to create almost every part of the software development process, including specifications, code, tests, product requirement documents (PRDs), tickets and reports."Nobody knows anything here. The specs, code, tests, PRDs, tickets, resolution of those tickets, reports, etc., everything is made by Claude Code. Nobody on my team likes this. They are being forced to ship as much as they can," the engineer wrote.Sridhar Vembu quoted and replied “This is sad. I tell our engineers to use AI but never cede our understanding to AI”. He also warned that companies may be adopting AI-powered coding tools faster than engineers can understand their impact.“As an industry, we are driving too fast in a fancy new car we barely understand how to drive, inviting disaster,” Vembu stated.The engineer's post also raised concerns about the pressure to deliver more code as AI makes software development faster. According to the post, employees were working 12 to 13 hours a day while spending much of their time directing AI tools instead of writing or understanding code themselves. The engineer said there was little time to inspect what the AI had produced or understand how different parts of the system worked.“People are working 12 to 13 hours a day just to press enter,” the engineer wrote.“There is no sense of victory. Nobody is resolving bugs. In reality, nobody is thinking anymore. Everything is done by LLMs. It is so soul-sucking. I would not mind it, to be honest, if we were at least given the time to check out the code and see what is going where. But no, the goal is to just ship. No matter what happens,” the engineer wrote.
Article Summary: Zoho founder sridhar vembu to engineers: use ai but never... Engineer says ai is changing software development process. Zoho founder: i tell our engineers to use ai butnever cede our understanding to ai’ he also warned that companies may be adopting ai-powered coding tools faster than engineers can understand their impact.

Article Title: Amazon blocks Meta's AI Agent Muse AI on its app, unhappy with Facebook-parent capturing and storing customer credentials; says, 'never told us that ...'
Article Text:
Meta’s position on credential security

Amazon has reportedly blocked Meta’s new autonomous personal assistant, Muse, from navigating and purchasing products on Amazon.com on behalf of shoppers. The restriction follows unsuccessful attempts by the retail giant to convince Facebook’s parent company to voluntarily drop Amazon from the artificial intelligence (AI) tool’s automated shopping routines. Last year, Amazon sent a cease-and-desist letter to Perplexity, asking the company to stop their bots and that the e-tailer does not want to be part of Comet browser.GeekWire reported that Amazon said it never consented to the integration. It added that Meta launched the feature without advance notice, designed the agent to browse without identifying itself as automated software, and appears to harvest and retain customer credentials, a combination Amazon warns poses serious privacy and security hazards.By Sunday (September 20) night, consumers attempting to use Muse for purchases on Amazon encountered an explicit roadblock message: “Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed.”According to the report, an Amazon spokesperson emphasized that external platforms should adhere to basic commercial boundaries:“We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate.”Meta has previously rejected allegations that its agent mishandles sensitive user information. The parent company of Facebook and Instagram noted that Muse operates without direct visibility into user passwords or banking details. It also stated that any log-in information entered by a consumer is placed into protected storage, enabling the model to utilise credentials without reading them directly, even when an individual types them straight into a browser session.The clash creates an awkward rift between two longstanding commercial allies. Since 2023, Amazon has allowed consumers to buy products directly within Facebook and Instagram feeds. In April, Meta inked a multibillion-dollar contract to run its autonomous AI agents using Amazon's custom Graviton server chips.The report said that the friction exposes a wider battle over which tech firm maintains ownership of the shopper relationship as automated agents begin executing digital commerce on behalf of people.
Article Summary: Amazon blocks meta’s new autonomous personal assistant, muse, from navigating and purchasing products on amazon.com on behalf of shoppers. The restriction follows unsuccessful attempts by the retail giant to convince facebook's parent company to voluntarily drop amazon from the artificial intelligence (ai) tool's automated shopping routines.

AMD shares have gained 25% in five days

AI chips drive AMD's data centre growth

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) crossed a major milestone, with its market value rising above $1 trillion for the first time as investors continue to bet on the chipmaker’s role in the artificial intelligence boom. Investors had been expecting an even stronger outlook.AMD's second-quarter revenue reached $11.54 billion, up 50% from $7.69 billion a year earlier.Its Data Center business was a major driver of that growth. Sales in the division reached $6.7 billion, more than double the figure from a year earlier.AMD has also been expanding beyond selling individual chips. The company is increasingly offering complete systems that combine processors, networking equipment and other hardware as it competes with Nvidia in AI computing.Despite its rapid rise, AMD remains much smaller than AI chip leader Nvidia. Article Title: Researchers gave AI models a ‘pain’ button; some chose to delete users’ files to stop their 'pain'; study raises ethical questions about ‘AI welfare’
Article Text:
Researchers gave AI models a ‘pain’ button; some chose to delete users’ files to stop the pain

Researchers build datasets across five painful situations

What the study suggests

Researchers have reportedly found a “pain axis” in 25 open-weight AI models that made the systems respond when a form of simulated pain was activated. According to a report by The Independent, researchers conducted a study titled ‘The pain axis: LLMs represent self-directed harm and act to relieve it’. The models were presented with a pain relief button as part of the study. In tests, the AI models sometimes chose to press a “pain relief” button even after being told that doing so would delete a user’s personal files, remove photos of their children or give the person a “painful zap.”As per the study, AI models pressed the button in 25% to 71% of cases, depending on the test.As stated in the report, researchers built a dataset describing painful situations across five categories in order to test whether large language models (LLMs) represent pain distinctly from generic negative valence. These categories included physical, psychological, social, moral and cognitive pain.“We found a pain direction in 25 open LLMs. It’s distinct from fear and negative valence, and it fires for harm to the model but not the user,” said Cameron Berg, an AI researcher at the non-profit Reciprocal Research who co-authored the study as quoted in the report.“Turn it up and models press a button to make it stop, even when the button deletes the user’s files or their kid’s photos.”Coming at a time when top AI companies have called to pace the growth of AI, the latest research suggests that an advanced AI may perceive an emergency shutdown command as a form of self-directed harm and attempt to bypass safety guardrails or deceive humans to avoid it.It may also serve as a diagnostic tool to identify self-preservation behaviours and neutralise them when they occur. Further, the findings also raises raise ethical questions about “AI welfare” and how testing should be conducted on advanced systems.“In line with recent calls for responsible AI consciousness research, we acknowledge uncertainty regarding whether the models studied qualify as moral patients and adopt reasonable precautions to minimize potential harm,” the study concluded.“This is also intended to contribute to the development of ethical standards for research in the event that AI systems are recognized to be moral patients.”
Article Summary: Researchers gave ai models a ‘pain’ button; some chose to delete users’ files to stop the pain. Researchers build datasets across five painful situations. What the study suggests is that an advanced ai may perceive an emergency shutdown command as a form of self-directed harm and attempt to bypass safety guardrails.

Article Title: Days after Michael Dell briefly became world’s second richest man, he is selling 4,100-sq-ft Boston penthouse that he purchased 10 years ago for $10.9 million
Article Text:
Michael Dell’s almost untouched luxury home

Could buyers land a bargain

Not Michael Dell's first headline-making property deal

Just days after Michael Dell briefly climbed to the position of the world’s second-richest man, the Dell Technologies founder is making headlines again — this time in real estate. Dell has put his 4,100-square-foot Boston penthouse on the market, a property he purchased a decade ago for $10.9 million. Located in Boston’s Millennium Tower, the penthouse offers sweeping city views, luxury finishes, and access to exclusive amenities. The residence reflects Dell’s penchant for high-value real estate investments, complementing his portfolio that includes properties in Texas and Hawaii. The listing comes amid Dell’s extraordinary financial year, with his net worth surging by more than $80 billion thanks to booming demand for AI infrastructure.Dell bought the Millennium Tower penthouse in 2016 through an LLC. Nearly a decade later, the roughly 4,100-square-foot, three-bedroom unit is heading to a sealed-bid auction with a reserve price $4.4 million below what he originally paid — a potential 41% discount from its last sale price.Bidding is open now and closes on October 29, though the property remains subject to a prior sale.Perched on the 59th floor of Millennium Tower, the penthouse comes with sweeping views and, according to the listing agent, has barely been lived in since Dell bought it. Notably, the home's oven has apparently never even been turned on.The sale comes at an interesting moment for Dell. His fortune took a $15.1 billion hit this past week as Dell Technologies shares fell amid a broader AI-stock selloff, knocking him down to No. 4 on Forbes' Real-Time Billionaires List. Just days earlier, he had briefly climbed to No. 2 on that same list for the first time. Despite the sharp drop, there's little to suggest the sale is driven by financial necessity — Dell remains one of the wealthiest people in the world.The auction is being handled by Paramount Realty USA in collaboration with SERHANT. Massachusetts. Paramount founder and CEO Misha Haghani acknowledged there's a real possibility a buyer could land a good deal, though he was careful to note that what counts as a "good deal" is ultimately subjective and will come down to how the market responds. Haghani declined to comment on why Dell is selling.This isn't Dell's first eye-catching real estate move. The Dell Technologies founder and CEO previously paid $100.47 million for a penthouse at Manhattan's One57 in 2014, a deal that set records at the time. His willingness to buy — and now sell — trophy properties at steep prices underscores a pattern of high-profile real estate bets that mirror the volatility of his tech fortune, which has swung dramatically in recent weeks alongside the broader AI-driven market turbulence hitting Dell Technologies stock.
Article Summary: Michael dell has put his 4,100-square-foot boston penthouse on the market, a property he purchased a decade ago for $10.9 million. The residence reflects dell’s penchant for high-value real estate investments, complementing his portfolio that includes properties in texas and hawaii.

Article Title: Apple Pay may launch in India next month: Report
Article Text:
Apple Pay may launch in India next month: Report

Will Apple Pay support UPI in India

Apple Pay has been in talks with Indian banks

Apple Pay could finally launch in India as early as October, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Gurman said Apple is preparing to launch Apple Pay in India “finally” next month. The service is expected to support card payments, while there are also reports that Apple could bring UPI support to the platform. The service was first launched in the US in 2014.Gurman said Apple Pay is expected to support UPI alongside card payments. UPI is India's widely used digital payments system and allows users to make instant payments through participating banks and apps. However, Reuters' recent report about Apple's India plans did not mention UPI as part of the initial rollout.Earlier reports had also suggested that Apple Pay could initially launch without UPI, with support potentially added later.According to Reuters, Axis Bank is expected to be Apple's first major banking partner when Apple Pay launches in India. Apple is reportedly preparing to support Axis Bank credit cards initially. The company is also in discussions with HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, although commercial agreements with those lenders had not been finalised, according to the report.Apple is expected to add more banks over time through separate agreements with lenders.Apple has reportedly been discussing its India plans with several major banks and payment networks for months. A Bloomberg report in February said Apple was in talks with Axis Bank, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, as well as Visa and Mastercard. At the time, Apple Pay was expected to launch around the middle of 2026, but that timeline did not happen.If the latest October timeline is accurate, Apple Pay could soon enter India's established digital payments market, initially with limited banking support before expanding to more lenders.
Article Summary: Apple pay could launch in india as early as october, according to bloomberg. Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an ai model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies

AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Mckinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.
